Senator Nangle, distinguished members of the
transportation committee, l'm Gary Drinkwater representing district 27, the towns of Alton, Argyle, Bradford, Corinth, Hudson, and Milford.
|'m here today to preset LD 516, an act to name the
bridge in Milford the Alton Drinkwater memorial
bridge. My father came from a family of 14. Dad was
born in 1926 and raised in Hampden, Maine. His mom
and dad never achieved the American dream of owning a home, they moved often and finally settled in
a home that was owned by his grandfather. At the age
of 10 (during the great depression) he walked with his
older brother to the first selectman's home to askfor a
voucher so they could get their mom some flour,
sugar, and other essentials. When the first selectman gave them the voucher, he told my dad and his brother,

Hampden doesn't need people like you living here.
He never forgot that experience.
He enlisted in the Navy in 1946 and sent money home
to help the family and asked his sister Helen to put
some money away for him. When he was discharged in1954, he came home and asked his sisterfor his
money, and was told she loaned it to her husband, and brother-in-law for truck repairs. He was never repaid.
Here he was, no money, no job, and no place to stay.
He had every right to be bitter, but he loved his
brothers and sisters and never let anything divide
them. Years later, when Aunt Helen's house burnt
down, with no insurance, 3 boys and a husband, he
stepped up with his two brothers and built them a new home with no mortgage.
In 1955 we moved to Milford where mom and dad
bought a house. It was there dad started Drinkwater's Auto Sales. He joined the Masons, volunteered in many organizations, served as a deacon, trustee, in
our church.

I remember in the early 70s a family that we didn't know came into the office. Upon introducing himself the man said, I moved to Milford with the
understanding that I had a job, my family and I have
been here two months staying at the Milford motel,
and thejob never materialized. I am here because I
don't have enough money to buy gas to get back to
Massachusetts. Without hesitation dad pulled out his
wallet and gave the man money for gas and food. The
gentleman thanked him and said, "l can't take it
without giving you something in return. Dad refused
but he insisted, so we ended up with a television. Dad never forgot what it was to be poor.
When the town of Milford wanted a new pick up for the
fire department, dad gave them one, when the local Elks club was starting, Dad provided them with an
automobile to raffle off.
Dave Georgia our local game warden, wanted to start a camp for kids, now called Maine's Youth Fish and
Game Association, dad gave them financial
assistance, and every year donated to the auction.
Most years he gave them a kayak, paddle, life jacket,

fishing rod and reel, and asked that it be raffled off to a
child. It was a pleasure watching a child's excitement when they had the winning ticket. If you were to visit
the club, you would see a plague dedicated to him. In
1998 Old Town High School needed money for lights for Victory field, and for the sports program. He gave
willingly of his time and money.
Growing up in the neighborhood we had two autistic brothers who stopped at the garage one day with a flat
bicycle tire. Dad asked them if they wanted a little job.
Those little jobs lasted for 15 years.
I must share this story of Arthur the older brother, who
is now deceased. Arthur would wash cars and mow
the lawns. One day down by the road a school bus
stopped at the railroad crossing, and traffic light. It
was early spring, and the bus had lots of kids. One kid
yelled out the open window "hey hog man". Arthur was
one who couldn't take any kidding, he immediately
yelled back you ca n't call me that. We all know what
happens when you tell kids you can't do that, they all
started yelling "hog man". Arthur walked over to the

bus and put that water hose in the open window and
started spraying everyone on the bus.
I could go on and on with stories, but I will end with
this, we lost Dad in 2007, and he would not want me
telling his story as he was a humble man who walked
with God, and as President George H.W. Bush once talked about "a thousand points of light," referring to
volunteerism, my father was one of those points.
I hope you agree with me and pass LD 516.

To the members of the Transportation Committee:
My name is Nathan Reimensnyder and I am a resident of New Gloucester. I am writing to testify in strong support of LD 511.
This is an pivotal point in our time regarding the protection and preservation of access to natural spaces in Maine. As more land is developed for private use, less is available for those around it. Having this rail trail through my community would be an incredible resource for me, my family, and my community.
New Gloucester is mostly rural with little to no available shoulder space and mostly 40+ MPH speed limits. This greatly limits our ability to enjoy riding bikes and walking/running in our area and especially so when including our 7 year old. The proposed trail would provide a safe space for us to take family bike rides and walks without having to worry about cars or trucks at all times. As a avid runner, I have experienced more than enough scary situations with distracted drivers.
Growing up in the area, the Royal River was an amazing feature to our town. One incredible aspect of the proposed trail would be its proximity to the river and the views and access it would provide. The views it would provide along this natural resource are some of the best in southern Maine, and access would allow for activities such as fishing and canoeing in the summertime and skating in the winter time. Overall, from a personal standpoint, my family and I would utilize this trail on a daily basis!
From a community standpoint, this trail would allow free access to natural spaces to those who aren't fortunate enough to have private access of their own. It would serve as a social hub, providing a safe outdoor space for our community to strengthen and grow. This trail would also serve as a significant attraction to visitors who would patronize our local businesses.
An interim trail from Portland to Auburn would improve public health, protect the environment, connect to public transit, and provide options for people who don't drive, or simply want to drive less. I firmly believe this is an incredible opportunity for our community and urge the committee members to vote "ought to pass."
Thank you for listening!
Nathan Reimensnyder
